claims.text: Formation of single-phase noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles is governed by the interplay of atomic size mismatch and electronic-structure compatibility.
Atomic size mismatch influences the energy landscape during nanoparticle nucleation and growth.
Electronic-structure compatibility influences the energy landscape during nanoparticle nucleation and growth.
Element substitution can systematically vary atomic size mismatch while preserving the number of elements and their overall compositional ratio.
Element substitution can systematically vary electronic-structure compatibility while preserving the number of elements and their overall compositional ratio.
Slow heating and cooling minimize kinetic effects during synthesis.
Slow heating and cooling allow thermodynamic factors to dominate formation and structure selection.
Atomic size mismatch creates lattice strain.
Electronic-structure compatibility affects bonding among the constituent elements.
Electronic-structure compatibility affects electronic energy states.
Lattice strain and electronic compatibility jointly determine the thermodynamic stability of the single-phase solid solution.
Lattice strain and electronic compatibility jointly determine crystal-structure selection.
Compositions with lower atomic size mismatch and higher electronic-structure compatibility will more readily form a single-phase solid solution with a well-defined crystal structure.
Higher atomic size mismatch and lower electronic-structure compatibility will increase the likelihood of phase separation.
Higher atomic size mismatch and lower electronic-structure compatibility will increase the likelihood of elemental segregation.
Higher atomic size mismatch and lower electronic-structure compatibility will increase the likelihood of amorphous structures.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements under slow, controlled heating and cooling.
